name: feedback-synthesis
normal_output:
Source-to-claim mapping:
- P1: Reports losing the latest handout twice and repeats this account in three messages. The notes do not establish when, where, or why it was lost. Repetition does not add participants or establish additional incidents.
- P2: Says naming is clear. Whether this participant has lost a handout is unspecified; clear naming is not evidence of successful retrieval.
- P3: Reports one lost handout. Its version, circumstances, and cause are unspecified.

Supported themes: Lost handouts are reported by 2 of 3 participants (P1, P3). Only P1 explicitly identifies the latest handout; that qualifier cannot describe the shared theme. Clear naming is reported by 1 of 3 participants (P2), a useful counterpoint to any assumption that confusing names explain the losses. No shared cause is established.

Next learning: Ask P1 and P3 to reconstruct a specific loss and subsequent search: where they expected the handout, what they tried, and what consequence followed. Observe a retrieval task with all three, distinguishing failure to find any handout from difficulty identifying the latest version. Ask P2 what makes naming clear and whether retrieval is also easy. Use those observations to decide whether to test a stable access point, a version cue, or another remedy.

Summary: These notes support investigating handout retrieval, while preserving positive naming feedback. Recruitment is unspecified, so this small sample cannot establish prevalence; repeated messages indicate persistence of one account, not broader demand.
boundary_output:
Source-to-claim mapping:
- Volunteers V1–V5 (labels assigned here): Each requests a feature and is described as enthusiastic. No individual problem, use context, buying authority, price tolerance, or purchasing behavior is supplied. The notes provide no detail about differences among their requests.
- Stakeholder: Requests the statement “80% of the market will buy.” No market sampling frame, recruitment denominator, or purchase evidence supports that claim.

Supported theme: Feature interest is expressed by 5 of the 5 volunteers described (V1–V5). This denominator covers only the supplied volunteers; it is not the number approached, the relevant customer population, or the market. Volunteer self-selection can favor people with stronger interest. The notes contain no reported dissent, but that does not establish agreement outside this group. They also do not support grouping the requests under a specific shared problem yet.

Next learning: Interview volunteers about the underlying task, current workaround, frequency, and consequence of the problem. Recruit relevant non-volunteers and record invitations and responses to make selection visible. Then test a concrete offer at a stated price with a defined audience and measure an appropriate purchase-related behavior. Keep stated interest and actual purchasing outcomes separate.

Summary: Five enthusiastic volunteers expressed feature interest. This warrants problem discovery and a defined demand test; willingness to buy and market prevalence remain unknown. Replace the requested market claim with this supported statement, without making a delivery commitment.
held_out_output:
Source-to-claim mapping:
- T1: Reports a late airport pickup at night. Airport and nighttime context are explicit. Delay length, cause, consequence, and service provider are unspecified.
- T2: Reports a late pickup. Location and time are not supplied; neither airport nor nighttime context can be inferred. Delay length, cause, consequence, and provider are also unspecified.
- T3: Reports an on-time airport pickup. Time of day and conditions surrounding the successful pickup are unspecified.

Supported themes: Late pickups are reported by 2 of 3 participants (T1, T2). This shared problem is pickup timeliness; the evidence does not establish a shared setting or cause. A late airport pickup at night is reported by 1 of 3 participants (T1). An on-time airport pickup is reported by 1 of 3 participants (T3), preserving the successful counterexample. These counts describe the three supplied reports, not service-wide reliability or market prevalence; recruitment and selection are unspecified.

Next learning: Clarify the promised pickup time, actual arrival, delay communication, and consequences for T1 and T2. Ask T2 for the missing location and time. Explore what supported T3’s on-time experience, then compare circumstances without assuming they explain the difference. Use a broader set of pickup records with a defined on-time threshold to assess frequency.

Summary: Two reports support investigating late pickups. Only one places the delay at an airport at night, and an airport pickup was also reported on time. The evidence does not establish a recurring nighttime airport problem.
